newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-BTPs to pause on way to 200 bp barrier.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-BTPs to pause on way to 200 bp barrier.

text.p: Italian BTPs, one of a trio of high-flying high-yield markets, will slow down in the short term but all signs point to further spread narrowing against German Bunds later this year, analysts said on Thursday.
An unexpectedly swift cut in Italian interest rates on Wednesday -- following tame inflation data -- failed to generate the sparks that have propelled BTPs throughout the year.
But investors will not have to wait long before BTPs start off again and cut the gap to 200 basis points or fewer amid the prospect of further interest rate cuts, analysts said.

"If, as I expect, the inflation differential continues to narrow, the same will happen with yield spreads," said Alfredo Granata, economist at Banca di Roma in Rome. "By the end of the year we could break the 200 basis point threshold."

Benchmark 10-year Italian BTPs yielded 214 basis points more than comparable Bunds at 1215 GMT. That gap, which has fallen from 228 at the beginning of the week, has more than halved from 475 at the start of the year.
Granata said BTPs' progress in spread terms would also be aided by an expected increase in long-term German yields.

In the past, high-yielding markets such as Italy, Sweden and Spain often depended on bullish bond markets to pare their yield premiums. But after improvement in a range of economic areas, yields in these markets nowadays are able to fall even when German yields are rising, analysts said.

"It will be difficult over the next two to four weeks to converge much further and sustain a move below 230 until we see the budget passed and Italy in the ERM," said Ifty Islam, European bond strategist at Merrill Lynch in London. "So we are seeing some consolidation in the general trend of convergence."

Membership of the ERM (Exchange Rate Mechanism) currency grid is one of the conditions for joining a single currency bloc. Italy left the ERM in 1992 amid intense speculative pressure against the lira.

But while some European authorities have been downplaying the likelihood or wisdom of Italy joining a single currency at the 1999 start date, Islam said markets would still focus on the chance of Italy joining anyway, albeit possibly at a later date.
"That's the basis for which we'd expect the trend of convergence to continue next year to 200 bp or lower," he said.
Craig Shute, economist at Bear Sterns International in London, also said a more bullish tone will emerge later.

"As people reflect on what has happened in Italy recently, with a set of good inflation data...they will probably reflect (on BTPs) more positively," he said. "So we may see more deft footwork by the Bank of Italy on cutting interest rates as we go into year end."
The Bank of Italy cut its discount rate to 7.5 percent from 8.25 percent on Wednesday. This followed a 75 basis point reduction in July.
Granata said that markets would increasingly focus on Italy's improving inflation differential with Germany, which was now down to nearly 150 basis points.

He said Italy had made long-term progress in the fight against inflation, noting improved efforts at getting industry to tighten margins rather than pass on higher costs and the effect of the lira's recovery.

Islam said he thought bond investors would look at a variety of factors in deciding whether to bet on further convergence, including issues such as the lira's potential ERM entry rate and the possible credit risk in Italy in a post-EMU environment.
In the short term, he said the main risk to BTP spread convergence was that the dollar would retreat against the mark, which would weigh on the lira.
